weeks.title: Nvidia shoots up, what does the bond market say?
weeks.overview: Summaries on the biggest theme across all four regions this week.

north-america.equities: Bonds and stocks are a little too connected in this piece, so it'll be shown in both equities and macro this week. Nvidia shot up 31.5% upon Jensen's return as CEO, with the S&P 500 having its best day in 19 months. The NASDAQ recovered as well. The bonds market didn't buy it. The US 10 -year Treasury Yield did not move. When market sentiment is that stocks have more upside, money tends to go into the stock market and exit the safe, stable bond market. This pushes rates high with the sell-off. What happened here was that investors put money into stocks but did not sell their safe bonds.  This signals to me that it was more relief about Nvidia and the Ai trade, rather than an optimistic outlook on the economy.

uk.equities: On Thursday, US tobacco group Altria said it is "considering a possible all-cash offer" for Imperial Brands. It is also in talks with another party over part of the Bristol-based group's business. Imperial shares rose 13.3%, their biggest one-day percentage gain on record, to a more than nine-year high. They added 1.8% on Friday, valuing the company at roughly £26bn. Under UK takeover rules, Altria has until 5pm on December 24 to make a firm offer or walk away. The approach comes after a weak year for Imperial, whose operating profit fell 10%, and adds to a run of foreign takeovers of London-listed companies. The bid helped lift the FTSE 100 1.8%, with miners and banks also gaining. This differs greatly from what is being seen in the US, with big tech causing chaotic swings in the NASDAQ and S&P 500. The FTSE 100 finished the week up 3.4%, its biggest weekly gain in eight months.
uk.macro: The Bank of England finished its review of capital rules for banks on Thursday.  Tier 1 requirement, the minimum amount of the highest quality capital a bank must hold, will fall by 50 basis points of risk-weighted assets for the biggest UK banks. UK-foucsed lenders get bigger cuts. The BoE warned that cutting much further would risk financial instability - pointing to fast growing AI-related debt, with hyperscaler bond issuance set to pass $305bn this year. The 10-year gilt has risen 40 basis points since July, mainly because markets expect higher interest rates. The Financial Times has shown that the US and UK have opposing economic problems: The US has had strong growth and a growing economic inequality issue, whereas the UK has had and is having a problem in their actual growth. I believe the BoE's view is that lending should be increased in order to promote growth, and decreasing capital requirements is an avenue for this.
